course.title: AP United States History
course.description: A vertical-video APUSH course organized as units, chapters, lessons, and instructional scenes.
course.audience: APUSH students preparing for class assessments and the AP exam

presentation.visual_style: museum-documentary visuals with readable AP exam vocabulary

units.title: Period 1: Worlds Before and After Contact
units.description: Indigenous societies before European arrival, Atlantic exploration, the Columbian Exchange, and the first Spanish systems of conquest and labor.
learning_objectives: Explain how geography shaped diverse Indigenous societies before European contact.
Explain the causes and effects of European exploration in the Americas.
Evaluate how the Columbian Exchange transformed societies on both sides of the Atlantic.

chapters.title: Labor, Debate, and Resistance
chapters.description: The Spanish labor systems that powered the colonial economy, the moral debate over conquest at Valladolid, Indigenous resistance that succeeded at Pueblo, and a review lesson that teaches Unit 1 as exam technique.
essential_questions: How did coerced labor systems sustain the Spanish colonial economy?
Why did the conquest of the Americas produce both a moral crisis and Indigenous resistance?
learning_objectives: Explain how the encomienda system worked and why it gave way to enslaved African labor.
Summarize the positions in the Valladolid debate and explain its historical significance.
Use the Pueblo Revolt and exam reasoning processes to build Unit 1 arguments.

lessons.title: From Encomienda to Slavery
lessons.description: The Spanish labor systems that built the colonial economy: encomienda, demographic collapse, and the turn to enslaved African labor.
lessons.essential_question: Who did the work of empire, and why did the answer change?
learning_objectives: Describe how the encomienda system granted and justified claims to Indigenous labor.
Explain how disease and overwork produced a labor shortage in the Spanish colonies.
Trace the economic logic that connected the dying Indigenous workforce to the transatlantic slave trade.

key_terms.definition: A Spanish labor grant giving a colonist the right to demand labor and tribute from Indigenous communities, justified as protection and Christian instruction.
The rapid, massive decline of Indigenous populations after contact, driven chiefly by Afro-Eurasian diseases to which they had no immunity.
The forced transport of enslaved Africans to the Americas to supply the colonial labor that Indigenous workers could no longer provide.

narration.text: [beat] Conquest is a story about soldiers, [emphasis]but empire is a story about workers[/emphasis]. Silver had to be mined, sugar had to be cut, fields had to be planted. The question that built the Spanish Empire was not who would rule. It was who would do the work. And the answer Spain gave changed the Americas forever.

animation.title: Who Does the Work of Empire?

source.title: Historical depiction of the encomienda system
source.notes: Use as historical evidence with attention to the creator's perspective.

scenes.production_notes: Open on the labor question; hold the essential question on screen before the definition.

narration.text: Spain's answer was the [es]encomienda[/es]: a royal grant giving a colonist the right to [emphasis]demand labor and tribute[/emphasis] from Indigenous communities. In exchange, the grantee promised protection and Christian instruction. [beat] It sounded orderly on paper. In practice, it became a system of [emphasis]forced labor that[/emphasis] enriched settlers and devastated Indigenous villages.

animation.title: The Encomienda: Promise vs. Practice
bullets: Royal grant: claims to Indigenous labor and tribute
animation.footer: AP Concept: Systems of coerced labor

source.title: Historical depiction of the encomienda system
source.notes: Distinguish the legal justification from documented practice.

scenes.production_notes: Reveal one bullet per narration clause; end on the contrast between justification and reality.

narration.text: [solemn]Then the workforce began to die. European diseases like smallpox swept through communities with no immunity, and brutal working conditions raised the death toll further. [beat] With Indigenous labor collapsing, Spanish planters and mine owners turned to [emphasis]enslaved Africans[/emphasis]. A cruel economic calculation that built the transatlantic slave trade.

animation.prompt: A casta painting labeled de Mulato y China sale Cambujo, showing a colonial labor landscape. Warm wind stirs the grass and leaves; thin smoke drifts upward in the distance; dust moves through shafts of sunlight; clouds glide slowly overhead. The engraved composition stays fixed and unchanged. Do not add people or buildings or text or modern objects.
animation.caption: Disease collapsed the workforce; enslaved African labor replaced it

source.title: Historical depiction of colonial labor
source.notes: Present the turn to enslaved labor as an economic mechanism; never as a natural outcome.

scenes.production_notes: Solemn tone; the clip animates the landscape, not the laborers.

narration.text: By the late 1500s, coerced labor was the engine of the colonial economy. Encomienda workers and enslaved Africans produced the silver and sugar that funded Spain's empire. [refrain]Remember the pattern for the exam: conquest created the demand, disease created the shortage, and slavery was the system's answer.[/refrain]

animation.title: The Labor System as a Causal Chain

source.title: Historical depiction of the encomienda system
source.notes: The diagram is a causal summary, not a timeline of every labor institution.

scenes.production_notes: Build the chain node by node; end on the exam pattern students should memorize.

lessons.title: Who Had the Right?
lessons.description: The 1550 Valladolid debate: Las Casas's written account forces the trial, Sepúlveda steelmans his case, Las Casas answers from his writing desk, and the verdict is a language, not a victory.
lessons.essential_question: Could the conquest of the Americas be morally justified?
learning_objectives: Summarize Sepúlveda's argument from natural slavery and its Aristotelian roots.
Explain Las Casas's defense of Indigenous peoples, including his tragic early irony.
Evaluate why the debate changed little on the ground but mattered for the history of rights.

key_terms.definition: The 1550–51 council debate at Valladolid, Spain, over the justice of Spain's conquest of the Americas.
Sepúlveda's Aristotelian claim that some peoples are slaves by nature and may justly be ruled by force.
The idea first articulated at Valladolid that conquest itself can be judged by universal moral law.

narration.text: [solemn]Look at this engraving. [beat] Made decades later to illustrate Bartolomé de Las Casas's account of the conquest, it shows Spanish soldiers torturing bound captives suspected of hiding gold. [beat] It was his words, carried across the Atlantic, that landed on the conscience of an empire. In [date:1550], Spain did what no Christian empire had ever done. [emphasis]It put itself on trial.[/emphasis]

beats.text: Who had the right to rule?

source.title: Theodor de Bry engraving, 1598
source.notes: Illustrating Las Casas's Destruction of the Indies; the images that forced the debate.

scenes.production_notes: Host opens ON the image: 'Look at this engraving' must land as the camera pushes in.

narration.text: [fierce]I never crossed the Atlantic, and I did not need to. [beat] Aristotle settled this two thousand years ago: [emphasis]some peoples are slaves by nature.[/emphasis] [beat] War against such peoples is just. It brings them Christianity, law, and order. [beat] Look at the mines. [slow]This is not cruelty. This is nature, doing its work.[/slow]

animation.title: Sepúlveda's Case
bullets: Just war brings Christianity and order

source.title: Theodor de Bry, Indigenous mine labor at Potosí, 1590
source.notes: The human cost Sepúlveda's argument justified; his case at full strength before the rebuttal.

scenes.production_notes: Sepúlveda cold and precise. 'Look at the mines' lands on the engraving; let the horror sit.

narration.text: [fierce:1.5]I was there. [beat] Fifty years in the Indies. I saw what Aristotle never saw. [beat] Look at my desk. [emphasis]This quill[/emphasis] has written more truth than Sepúlveda's whole library. These are not natural slaves. They are [emphasis]rational souls[/emphasis], capable of faith and self-rule. [beat] His so-called just war is theft with a Latin blessing.

source.title: Bartolomé de Las Casas at his writing desk, engraving, 1791
source.notes: Callouts mark what the narration names: quill, cross, papers.

scenes.production_notes: Las Casas answers point by point. Hard cut in; the callouts are already up when he says 'Look at my desk.'

narration.text: [solemn]Valladolid changed almost nothing on the ground. The mines ground on. The encomienda ground on. [beat] But it invented something new: the idea that conquest itself could be judged. Judged by [emphasis]universal moral law.[/emphasis] [beat] That language, of [slow]natural rights and human dignity[/slow], would outlive the empire it failed to restrain.

animation.prompt: A historical engraved portrait of Bartolome de las Casas resting in a quiet chamber. A candle flame flicker softly nearby; its light shimmer shifts gently across the dark background; fine dust drifts through the air; a faint mist hangs near the frame. The portrait itself remains unchanged and the composition holds steady. Do not add people or text or modern objects.

source.title: Bartolomé de Las Casas at his writing desk, engraving, 1791
source.notes: The verdict: a language, not a victory.

scenes.production_notes: The stamp lands on 'natural rights'; let the final line breathe.

lessons.title: 1680: The Revolt That Worked
lessons.description: The Pueblo Revolt of 1680: causes, Popé's organization, the expulsion of the Spanish, and what it proved about Indigenous agency.
lessons.essential_question: Why did the Pueblo Revolt succeed where other resistance failed?
learning_objectives: Identify the causes of the Pueblo Revolt: mission labor, drought, and religious repression.
Describe how Popé organized the revolt across Pueblo villages.
Explain what the revolt's success shows about Indigenous agency and the limits of empire.

key_terms.definition: The 1680 Pueblo uprising led by Popé that expelled the Spanish from New Mexico for twelve years.
A Pueblo religious leader who organized the 1680 revolt village by village.
The Spanish colonial institution that combined religious conversion with coerced Indigenous labor.

narration.text: [awed]In August 1680, in the deserts of New Mexico, Indigenous people did something that never happened anywhere else in North America: [emphasis]they completely expelled the colonizers[/emphasis]. The Pueblo Revolt is the only fully successful Native uprising in the continent's history. And it kept the Spanish out for twelve years.

source.title: Historical depiction of a Spanish mission
source.notes: The missions were the labor system the revolt targeted; use the image for setting, not as a battle scene.

scenes.production_notes: Cold open on the superlative; hold twelve years on screen as the hook's payoff.

narration.text: The causes built for eighty years. [beat] Spanish missions demanded heavy labor while suppressing Pueblo religion; drought strained every village; and colonial governors punished native ceremonies as witchcraft. [fierce]Into this anger stepped [es]Popé[/es], a religious leader who carried a message village to village: [emphasis]drive out the Spanish, and return to the old ways[/emphasis].

source.title: Historical depiction of a Spanish mission
source.notes: The timeline is a causal summary; missions, drought, and repression overlapped rather than sequencing neatly.

scenes.production_notes: Advance one event per cause; land Popé as the organizing force, not a lone hero.

narration.text: [urgent]In August 1680 the revolt exploded. Pueblo warriors struck across New Mexico, killed hundreds of settlers, and besieged Santa Fe until the Spanish fled south to El Paso. [beat] The victory was total. And it held. For twelve years, the Pueblo peoples [emphasis]governed themselves[/emphasis], free of missions, taxes, and Spanish law.

animation.prompt: A Spanish mission church and its courtyard under a desert sky. Clouds drift slowly overhead; wind stirs dust across the courtyard; dry leaves sway on the few trees; light smoke curls from a distant chimney. Shadows move gently over the walls. The scene stays fixed and unchanged. Do not add people or text or modern objects.
animation.caption: August 1680: the Spanish are expelled; twelve years of independence follow

source.title: Historical depiction of a Spanish mission
source.notes: Animate the place, not the battle; no image here depicts the fighting itself.

scenes.production_notes: The clip is ambient desert motion; the violence belongs in the narration, not the visuals.

narration.text: The Pueblo Revolt proved two things the textbooks used to miss. [beat] First, Indigenous peoples were [emphasis]not passive victims[/emphasis] of conquest. They organized, planned, and won. Second, even the strongest empire had limits. [slow]Resistance was not just a footnote to colonization; sometimes, it rewrote the story.[/slow]

animation.title: What the Revolt Proved
bullets: Indigenous peoples organized, planned, and won
Even the strongest empire had limits
Resistance was not a footnote — it rewrote the story
animation.footer: AP Skill: Causation + Continuity and Change

source.title: Historical depiction of a Spanish mission
source.notes: Close the unit arc here: resistance as historical force, not epilogue.

scenes.production_notes: Defiant lift, matching the plan's closer; end Unit 1 on Indigenous agency.

lessons.title: Unit 1 Review: Think Like the Exam
lessons.description: An exam-technique review of Unit 1: the unit thesis, the three reasoning processes, the Fall 2026 SAQ format, and DBQ/LEQ habits that earn the points students most often lose.
lessons.essential_question: How do you turn Unit 1 knowledge into exam points?
learning_objectives: State the Unit 1 thesis and attach each major topic to it as evidence.
Apply the three reasoning processes — comparison, causation, continuity and change — to Unit 1 material.
Describe how to answer each Fall 2026 SAQ type and which DBQ/LEQ habits earn the most-lost points.

key_terms.definition: Short-Answer Question: three required questions on the APUSH exam (Q1 secondary text, Q2 primary text, Q3 non-text), each scored 0–3 with A/B/C independent.
Document-Based Question: a 7-point essay built from seven documents plus outside evidence, analysis, and sourcing.
Placing an argument in its broader historical setting — one of the points students lose most often on the LEQ.

narration.text: Unit 1 has a thesis you can state in one sentence: [refrain]geography wrote the first draft of American history, and contact rewrote it[/refrain]. [beat] Environment shaped the societies of 1491; European motives brought sustained contact; the Columbian Exchange redistributed disease, wealth, and labor. Everything else in the unit is [emphasis]evidence for that claim[/emphasis].

animation.title: The Unit 1 Thesis in One Minute

source.title: Unit 1 contextual image
source.notes: Review lesson: visuals cue memory; the argument does the teaching.

scenes.production_notes: This is exam technique, not a rehash — every line should point at how students will use it.

narration.text: The exam tests three reasoning processes, and Unit 1 gives you all three. [fast]Comparison: set two societies side by side and argue similarity or difference. Causation: trace how one change produced another, like disease enabling conquest. Continuity and change: labor systems evolved, but coerced labor persisted.[/fast] [beat] [emphasis]Name the process, then use it.[/emphasis]

animation.title: The Three Reasoning Processes on Unit 1
bullets: Comparison: two societies, similarity or difference
Continuity and change: what evolved, what persisted
animation.footer: AP Skill: name the process, then use it

source.title: Unit 1 contextual image
source.notes: Each reasoning process maps to a Unit 1 example students have already seen.

scenes.production_notes: Pause on each process long enough for students to attach their own example.

narration.text: On the Fall 2026 exam, all three S-A-Qs are required. [beat] No choice. Question 1 gives you a secondary text: [emphasis]identify the author's argument[/emphasis]. Question 2 gives a primary text: explain what it shows about the period. Question 3 gives a non-text source, like a map or image: read it literally, then connect it to the topic.

animation.title: The Three SAQs: What Each One Wants
bullets: Q1 — secondary text: find the author's argument
Q2 — primary text: explain what it shows
Q3 — non-text: read the image, chart, or map
animation.footer: All 3 SAQs required — no choice (Fall 2026 CED)

source.title: SAQ set 06, question 3 stimulus
source.notes: Stimulus shown as a format example; teach students to read source type before content.

scenes.production_notes: Teach the SAQ move, not the content — this scene transfers to every unit.

narration.text: The D-B-Q is worth seven points and the L-E-Q six. [beat] And the Chief Reader's data shows exactly [emphasis]where students bleed[/emphasis]: sourcing at 0.39 out of 1, complex understanding at 0.15, evidence beyond the documents at 0.47. [slow]The fix is a habit, not talent:[/slow] source every document, bring one outside fact, and tie each piece of evidence to your argument.

animation.prompt: A historical painting of Columbus’s landing party on a tropical shore. Clouds drift slowly across the sky; tree leaves stir in a light breeze; water shimmers along the shoreline; dust drifts over the sand; the banner fabric ripples faintly in the wind. The painted scene stays unchanged and the frame holds steady. Do not add people or text or modern objects.
animation.caption: The points students lose most: sourcing, complex understanding, beyond-docs evidence

source.notes: Stats from the 2025 Chief Reader Report (APUSH_CONTENT_PLAN.md): sourcing 0.39/1, complex understanding 0.15/1, beyond-docs evidence 0.47/1.
